# Using MitER for 3D analysis of mitochondrial morphology and ER contacts

**Authors:** Therese Kichuk; Satyen Dhamankar; Saurabh Malani; William A. Hofstadter; Scott A. Wegner; Ileana M. Cristea; José L. Avalos

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Molecular Biology, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544, USA | 2Department of Chemical and Biological Engineering, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544, USA | 3The Andlinger Center for Energy and the Environment, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544, USA | 4High Meadows Environmental Institute, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544, USA | 5Omenn-Darling Bioengineering Institute, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544, USA

## Abstract

We have developed an open-source workflow that allows for quantitative single-cell analysis of organelle morphology, distribution, and inter-organelle contacts with an emphasis on the analysis of mitochondria and mitochondria-endoplasmic reticulum (mito-ER) contact sites. As the importance of inter-organelle contacts becomes more widely recognized, there is a concomitant increase in demand for tools to analyze subcellular architecture. Here, we describe a workflow we call MitER (pronounced “mightier”), which allows for automated calculation of organelle morphology, distribution, and inter-organelle contacts from 3D renderings by employing the animation software Blender. We then use MitER to quantify the variations in the mito-ER networks of Saccharomyces cerevisiae, revealing significantly more mito-ER contacts within respiring cells compared to fermenting cells. We then demonstrate how this workflow can be applied to mammalian systems and used to monitor mitochondrial dynamics and inter-organelle contact in time-lapse studies.

## Abstract

Mitochondrial morphology and contact with proximal organelles are important in both healthy and diseased cell states. Quantification of mitochondrial contact with the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is particularly valuable as these contacts influence numerous cellular processes, such as mitochondrial fission and fusion, mitophagy, and calcium signaling. However, there are limited tools for such quantitative analyses. Current open-source methods solely allow for colocalization measurements, which are sufficient to estimate inter-organelle contact but lack the ability to provide more substantial metrics, such as the surface area and number of discrete contacts.

## Abstract

Kichuk et al. introduce MitER, an open-source workflow that allows for quantitative single-cell analysis of organelle morphology, distribution, and inter-organelle contacts. The workflow is used to quantify the variations in the mitochondria-endoplasmic reticulum (mito-ER) networks of Saccharomyces cerevisiae, revealing a significant increase in mito-ER contacts within respiring cells compared to fermenting cells.

## Introduction

Mitochondria have long been known for their importance to normal cellular function. These organelles are responsible for cellular respiration, metabolism, and programmed cell death.1 Mitochondrial dysfunction and its associated morphological changes are common characteristics in numerous disease processes. Mitochondria, however, do not function independently of other organelles, and their behavior can be better understood through their interactions with other subcellular compartments. Mitochondria-endoplasmic reticulum (mito-ER) contacts are increasingly recognized for their importance in fundamental cellular processes and to the pathophysiology underlying numerous diseases. These contacts are hubs for lipid transport, calcium signaling, and mitophagy. Moreover, disruptions in these contact sites are implicated in the pathophysiology of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) and Parkinson’s disease.2,3

Recent studies of mito-ER contacts have been enabled by the visualization of mito-ER overlap in live cells with fluorescence microscopy.4 The availability of image analysis tools to analyze inter-organelle contact sites, however, lags behind the ability to collect high-quality imaging data. Open-source software like Fiji5 allows researchers to obtain colocalization measurements, but these measurements do not allow for meaningful characterization of mito-ER interactions. In mammalian cells, for example, 5%–20% of the mitochondrial surface is reported to be in contact with the ER,6 but little is known about the precise number of discrete contacts, or the surface area of each. Analysis of 3D electron tomography data has provided a more detailed picture of the size of these contacts,7 but acquiring these data can be challenging and the requirement to freeze the sample prohibits live-cell imaging.

In this study, we show how mitochondrial morphology and ER contacts in living yeast cells can be quantified in greater detail by using a 3D rendering-based approach to analyze fluorescence microscopy images. We leverage the open-source rendering software MitoGraph8 to obtain high-quality renderings of subcellular structures. Then, using the open-source animation software Blender,9 we measure various structural characteristics of these renderings. We automate this process in a workflow we call MitER that can be used to analyze microscopy images of live or fixed cells. Using standard confocal fluorescent images, MitER allows for the estimation of cell volume and surface area in addition to the determination of mitochondrial morphology and inter-organelle contact. Using MitER, we measure changes in mitochondrial surface area, mito-ER contacts, and mitochondrial distribution in Saccharomyces cerevisiae as cells switch from fermentation to respiration. Additionally, we employ MitER to investigate the dynamic behavior of these cells during this metabolic transition and demonstrate how this workflow can be applicable to mammalian systems. This method addresses the growing need for tools to analyze inter-organelle contacts, mitochondrial morphology, dynamics, and organelle localization.

## Results

### Sample preparation and image acquisition

We sought to design a versatile workflow for the analysis of confocal images of live or fixed cells (Figure 1). We were particularly interested in characterizing the phenotypic differences between the organelles of cells as they transitioned between metabolic states (Figure 1A). To do this we marked both the mitochondria and the ER of S. cerevisiae with fluorescent proteins (GFPmut3 and mCherry, respectively).10 We then obtained confocal images of approximately 30 cells per metabolic state in two different fluorescent channels (for GFP and mCherry) using a Nikon CSU-W1 SoRa (Figure 1B).Figure 1Experimental setup and MitER workflow(A) Yeast cells are grown to mid-exponential phase and then switched to fresh media with different carbon sources.(B) Following incubation, cells are imaged using confocal microscopy.(C) Confocal images are processed using a 3D rendering software (here MitoGraph), and single cells are segmented following rendering.(D) The cell surface is estimated using Delaunay 3D triangulation of the ER signal in ParaView. Following pre-processing, MitER is entirely automated.(E and F) Within Blender, the MitER script (E) detects the cell surface, ER, and mitochondria and (F) extracts information regarding the volume, surface area, and position of each object.(G) The program then computes mito-ER overlap and determines both the mitochondrial distribution and asymmetry within the cell.(H) The output from these measurements is finally processed and formatted using a separate R script.Figure was created with BioRender.com.gr1.jpg338965355cc3c1ee6736d0306fb85b563a1e54LOAD_COMPLETED25602972640743urn:cdn:blobs/d783/10832265/355cc3c1ee67/gr1.jpggr1.gif76058dc68388b89d311bd7edef7645c5e126dNEVER_LOAD86100urn:cdn:blobs/d783/10832265/dc68388b89d3/gr1.gif

### 3D segmentation allows for single-cell analysis of cell clusters

Although other rendering software can be used, we employed the open-source program MitoGraph to render both the mitochondrial and ER fluorescent signals within each cell (Figure 1C). By duplicating the defined region of interest (ROI) between channels, the resulting renderings preserve the spatial positioning of each organelle relative to one another. Because of the challenge of accurately defining 3D ROIs in Fiji, we opened the VTK files exported from MitoGraph in ParaView11 to further segment renderings of clusters containing between 2 and 3 cells. In this way, we ensured that downstream analysis would only be conducted on single cells regardless of whether or not the yeast was budding along the z-axis. This additional segmentation step allows us to select single cells along three axes, avoiding the need to resolve cells solely by a two-dimensional ROI. In this manner, 3D segmentation allows for more cells to be analyzed per image.

### Pre-processing in ParaView enables cell surface estimation from ER signal

Following 3D segmentation, the cell surface can be estimated by applying a Delaunay 3D filter to the ER mesh in ParaView. The output is a tetrahedral mesh approximating the outermost points of the ER rendering. Given that this organelle abuts the intracellular plasma membrane surface, this signal can serve as a proxy for the cell surface (Figure 1D). Estimation of the cell surface and the creation of this additional mesh allows for downstream analysis of three structures (ER, mitochondria, and cell surface) from only two fluorescent channels (ER and mitochondria). We found that the periphery of the ER signal is highly correlated to the cell surface during both fermentation and respiration. Cell volumes estimated by the ER signal are on average 85.4% of the volumes measured more accurately using a MemBrite cell-wall dye (approximately 85% and 86% for fermenting and respiring cells, respectively) (Figure S1). To account for this slight and consistent discrepancy, the MitER script scales the volume of the cell surface as estimated by the ER by 1.17× (calculated from the inverse of 0.854) to correct for the underestimation in cell volume. As a further quality control, we ensure that all cells used in downstream analysis contain 99% of their mitochondrial volume within the corrected cell perimeter. This excludes cells with very poor ER renderings such that the Delaunay 3D surface of these ER signals would not encapsulate the mitochondria.

The advantage of estimating the cell surface from the ER signal is that it eliminates the need for a dye, which avoids additional incubation steps that can interfere with cell physiology. This method also leaves an additional fluorescent channel available to mark other subcellular structures if needed. Once cells are segmented and the cell surface mesh is created, the scene containing the renderings of each subcellular component is exported as an .x3d file, which is compatible with the MitER workflow in Blender.

### Import into Blender and cell structure labeling

Although segmentation and pre-processing are manual, the remainder of the protocol is automated with minimal required user input. The program prompts the user to select the folder containing the .x3d files of each single-cell scene. These are then automatically imported and analyzed. Cell structures are detected and automatically labeled (Figure 1E). First, the program identifies the structure with the largest volume and recognizes it as the cell. Second, the ER is identified as the structure with the same bounding box (the smallest cuboid drawn around a set of points such that all the points are within that cuboid) dimensions as the cell surface but a smaller mesh volume. This labeling strategy is effective as the cell surface is computed from the ER surface and, therefore, both structures will share bounding box dimensions. The remaining structure is identified as the mitochondria. The automated workflow is also compatible with two structure systems where only the cell surface and a single additional organelle are marked. The structure with the smallest volume corresponds to the organelle in question whose asymmetry and distribution is analyzed based on the larger structure (assumed to be the cell surface).

### Obtaining measurements of cell components

A key benefit to using Blender for single-cell analysis is the ability to take advantage of native functions within the software for accurate surface area and volume measurements. Converting each organelle to a triangulated mesh object and correcting non-manifold geometries allows us to quickly and easily calculate the surface area and volume of each subcellular component (Figure 1F). More complicated cellular measurements such as Booleans used for computing intersections between objects (discussed below) can be aided by simplifying the mesh (by calling the Remesh modifier in Blender) and specifying a voxel size (here, we chose a voxel size of 0.03). At this voxel size, this operation preserves organelle volume and overall shape but simplifies the topology to improve downstream calculations using Boolean modifiers. In our study, each organelle surface mesh was made manifold, re-meshed using a voxel size of 0.03, and triangulated prior to volume and surface area measurements.

In addition to volume and surface area measurements, we can obtain information regarding the structure’s spatial dimensions by exporting bounding box vertices. The center of gravity of each mesh object in the scene is computed by assuming they have uniform density and finding the center of mass based on the volume. The number of individual mitochondria in addition to their volumes and surface areas are computed by splitting the mitochondrial channel by connected components such that each individual mitochondrion is identified as a separate object.

### Inter-organelle contact and organelle distribution

Blender also allows for the computation of object intersections. By applying the intersection Boolean modifier in Blender to the ER and mitochondria channels (which preserves only the overlapping components between these objects), we compute the number and volume of mito-ER contacts, and we determine the surface area of the contacts from the surface area of the overlap volumes (corrected by a factor of 0.5 so as to not double count the contact surface area) (Figures 1G and 2A). We also employ the intersection Boolean to quantify organelle distribution within the cell. To determine organelle distribution, we discretized the radial cumulative distribution function by scaling down the cell volume (making twenty concentric sections increasing by equal volumes while keeping the center the same) at various fractions between 0 and 1 (Figure 2B, left). We then used the resulting concentric shapes to section the cell, calling on the intersection Boolean function to compute the volume of the organelle of interest in each subsection. Because we are simply scaling the cell shape, this method can be extended to a variety of cellular morphologies.Figure 2Organelle distribution and inter-organelle contact(A) The intersection between the mitochondrial and ER meshes is determined using the native intersection Boolean function in Blender. A size filter can then be applied to these contacts in R to compensate for any potential noise.(B) To determine the organelle's spatial distribution, we discretize a cumulative distribution function by scaling down the cell volume (while maintaining the same cell center) at various fractions between 0 and 1; the intersection Boolean is then employed to determine the volumes of the mitochondria and ER in each cumulative subsection (concentric cell shapes).(C) Calculation of the organelle surface area within each subsection is performed using Equation 1.(D) Asymmetry of the mitochondrial distribution within the cell can be calculated by calculating the distance between the centers of gravity of the mitochondria and the cell (assuming uniform density) and normalizing by the cellular radius.Figure was created with BioRender.com.gr2.jpg2629683d96f1d7427d8169f32fbb6b6ac940d8LOAD_COMPLETED13172207439735urn:cdn:blobs/d783/10832265/3d96f1d7427d/gr2.jpggr2.gif74388c0c845eda639ec02a57adfef5969ec34NEVER_LOAD80134urn:cdn:blobs/d783/10832265/c0c845eda639/gr2.gif

### Analysis of cell measurements in R

The MitER pipeline outputs (1) organelle surface area, (2) organelle volume, (3) the volume of each inter-organelle contact, and (4) the surface area of the volume of each inter-organelle contact. Using a separate R script, we analyzed these raw data into useful metrics such as total contact count and the number of contacts above a user-defined volume cutoff. As mentioned above, the surface area of each contact site was derived in R by halving the surface area of the volume of the inter-organelle overlap with the assumption that the contact site has half of its surface abutting one organelle and the other half lining the other organelle. The organelle volume, the organelle surface area, and the inter-organellar surface area measurements in each subsection can be used to compute their subcellular distributions (Figure 2B).

MitER calculates both volume and surface area distributions to give the user options regarding their metric of interest. To calculate volume distributions, the organelle volume and contact volume in each subcellular subsection can be used directly as reported by Blender. To calculate surface area distributions, however, care must be taken to not include in the extra surface area created by the slicing of the organelle during cell subsectioning, as Blender interprets the sliced organelle as being a complete organelle. The true surface area of the organelle present in the section, S A o r g a n e l l e , is calculated with Equation 1.Equation (1) S A o r g a n e l l e = S A s e c t i o n + S A d i f f e r e n c e − S A s u r f a c e 2 , where S A s e c t i o n is the organelle surface area in the section reported by Blender, S A s u r f a c e is the surface area of the cell subsection, and S A d i f f e r e n c e is the resulting surface area when the organelle is subtracted from the sectioning shape (Figure 2C). The calculated distribution metrics can be used to describe complicated organelle characteristics such as situations in which there is predominantly central organelle volume, while the majority of the surface area is found toward the periphery of the cell.

The R script also computes the asymmetry in the organelle distribution by taking the Euclidean distance between the center of gravity of the cell and the center of gravity of the organelle components (Figure 2D). This is then normalized by the mean cell radius to yield a unitless number between 0 and 1, with 0 indicating perfect angular symmetry around the cellular center and 1 indicating maximal asymmetry.

### Comparison to current methods

To validate our approach, we compared our method against current gold-standard approaches. We compared the organelle volume measurements from the MitER workflow in Blender to the values obtained with MitoGraph and Imaris from the same renderings (Figures S2A and S2B). We found that our volume measurements agreed with those calculated by both MitoGraph and Imaris. Additionally, we compared the mitochondrial and ER surface area measurements calculated by MitER and Imaris (Figure S2C). Once again, we found complete agreement between the measurements reported by each method. As a final verification, we compared inter-organelle overlap volumes calculated by MitER with those reported by Imaris from the same renderings (Figure S2D). For any given yeast rendering, the outputs from MitER and Imaris are the same.

To validate the use of MitoGraph to estimate inter-organelle contacts, we compared MitER outputs using MitoGraph renderings to MitER outputs using Imaris renderings of the same cells (Figure S3). Specifically, we looked at the fraction of organelle volume (Figure S3A) accounted for by the volume of inter-organelle contact (contact volume/organelle volume). We then looked at the fraction of organelle surface area (Figure S3B) accounted for by the surface area of the overlap between the structures (contact surface area/organelle surface area). Using these measurements, we can find what fraction of the mitochondrial surface is in contact with the ER and vice versa. We found a strong correlation in the outputs between MitoGraph and Imaris renderings, confirming the validity of the open-source rendering method used in this study.

### MitER analysis of S. cerevisiae

To demonstrate the utility of MitER for a variety of mitochondrial morphologies, we analyzed S. cerevisiae cells during respiration, fermentation, and the transition from fermentation to respiration. Cells from overnight cultures were grown to mid-exponential phase in synthetic complete (SC) media containing either glucose (SC-Glu) or glycerol ethanol (SC-GE). Cells grown in SC-Glu were then used to inoculate fresh SC-Glu (fermentation) or SC-GE (transition), whereas cells grown in SC-GE were used to inoculate fresh SC-GE (respiration). After a minimum 3-h incubation at room temperature, the cells were imaged on a Nikon CSU-W1 SoRa (Figure 3A), and the images were processed as detailed above.Figure 3Analysis of mitochondrial volume in S. cerevisiae(A) Schematic of the experimental setup and representative data. Mitochondria were fluorescently tagged using COX4-GFP. The endoplasmic reticulum was marked using SS-mCherry-HDEL. Maximum intensity projections of single-cell z-stacks are displayed along with their corresponding renderings.(B) Mitochondrial volume as computed from the organelle renderings increases from fermentation to respiration.(C) Mitochondrial volume normalized to corrected cell volume increases from fermentation to respiration.(D) Correlation of total mitochondrial volume to corrected cell volume.ns: p > 0.05, ∗: p ≤ 0.05, ∗∗: p ≤ 0.01, ∗∗∗: p ≤ 0.001, ∗∗∗∗: p ≤ 0.0001.Figure was created with BioRender.com.gr3.jpg4419602393d610e83f06cf797b855bce0336f3LOAD_COMPLETED32612972815743urn:cdn:blobs/d783/10832265/2393d610e83f/gr3.jpggr3.gif780913339699dac9a7feabce60488efceea66NEVER_LOAD110100urn:cdn:blobs/d783/10832265/3339699dac9a/gr3.gif

It is well documented that there is an increase in mitochondrial volume as yeast cells switch from fermentation to respiration.12 As expected, we measured an increase in the absolute (Figure 3B) and normalized mitochondrial volume (Figure 3C) in respiring cells and, to a lesser degree, cells transitioning from fermentation to respiration. The mitochondrial volumes measured by MitER and the recorded trends between mitochondrial and cell volumes across media conditions agree with previous studies (Figure 3D).12

Following validation of MitER organelle measurements, we next investigated if different metabolic states contribute to differences in mito-ER contacts. We found the surface area of mitochondria increases as cells transition from fermentation to respiration (Figure 4A), while the surface area of the ER drops between fermentation and the transition state (Figure 4B). Interestingly, we observed a lower percentage of mitochondrial surface in contact with the ER as cells transitioned from fermentation to respiration (Figure 4C). This suggests that mitochondria increase in surface area (and volume) before forming new contacts with the ER as cells transition from fermentation to respiration. While the fraction of the mitochondrial surface area accounted for by ER contact is the same in respiration as in fermentation (Figure 4C), the fraction of ER surface contacting mitochondria is increased during the respiration state (Figure 4D). Notably, mito-ER interfaces have a greater total surface area in respiring cells relative to fermenting cells (Figure 4E) indicating either larger contact sites, a greater number of them, or both. Despite this increase into mito-ER surface area, however, the density of mito-ER contact sites (number of mito-ER contact sites normalized to mitochondrial surface area) is the same in fermentation and respiration though lower in transitioning cells (Figure 4F).Figure 4Mito-ER contacts in S. cerevisiae(A) Total mitochondrial surface area across growth conditions.(B) Total ER surface area across growth conditions.(C) Fraction of mitochondrial surface area in contact with the ER.(D) Fraction of the ER surface area in contact with mitochondria.(E) Total surface area of mitochondria-ER interfaces.(F) Mito-ER contact density.(G and H) A significant increase in mito-ER contacts from fermentation to respiration is apparent when examining either (G) total mito-ER contacts or (H) filtering out contact volumes that are below the theoretical limit of resolution.(I) To verify that the increase in mito-ER overlap is representative of an increase in real contact sites, we tagged the ERMES protein Mmm1 with GFP and imaged the cells.(J and K) We then rendered these images with MitoGraph, (J) counted the total individual puncta using the MitER script in Blender, and (K) filtered out contact volumes that were below the theoretical limit of resolution.ns: p > 0.05, ∗: p ≤ 0.05, ∗∗: p ≤ 0.01, ∗∗∗: p ≤ 0.001, ∗∗∗∗: p ≤ 0.0001.Figure was created with BioRender.com.gr4.jpg337505f5e5597ddb185f9379ae6796db7760caLOAD_COMPLETED28233321627738urn:cdn:blobs/d783/10832265/f5e5597ddb18/gr4.jpggr4.gif765997df76140d87b85fddb92ccb41e372c42NEVER_LOAD85100urn:cdn:blobs/d783/10832265/7df76140d87b/gr4.gif

Looking at individual mito-ER contact sites across conditions, we find an increase during respiration (Figures 4G and 4H). Even after excluding contacts smaller than 0.009 μm3 (computed from the theoretical resolution limit) to minimize noise introduced during live cell imaging (Figure 4H), there is a significant increase in the number of mito-ER contacts in respiration relative to both fermentation and cells transitioning from fermentation to respiration. MitER detected an average of 13.5 total contacts per fermenting cell but only an average of 6 contacts above 0.009 μm3 per fermenting cell. For respiring cells, MitER detected an average of 32 total contacts of which an average of 15 were above 0.009 μm3.

To verify that the MitER-measured increase in mito-ER overlap reflects a true increase in real mito-ER contact sites, we labeled the contact site protein Mmm1p with GFPmut3. Mmm1p is a crucial component of the ER-mitochondria encounter structure (ERMES), and clusters of 250 or more of these molecules light up as GFP puncta, showing the number of individual bona fide contact sites.13 We imaged these cells in both fermentative and respiratory states (Figure 4I) and observed more Mmm1-GFP puncta in respiring cells, confirming the results obtained with MitER. For further validation, we rendered the puncta using MitoGraph and counted the individual objects using MitER in Blender (Figures 4J and 4K). Using Mmm1p puncta (instead of computed mito-ER overlaps), MitER detected an average of 9 total mito-ER contacts per fermenting cell with an average of 6 contacts above 0.009 μm3. Analyzing Mmm1-GFP puncta in respiring cells, MitER detected an average of 16 total contacts with an average of 12 contacts above 0.009 μm3. Thus, analysis of individual Mmm1p-GFP clusters, indicating bona fide mito-ER contact sites, recapitulates the trend in mito-ER contacts observed with MitER analysis of two fluorescently tagged organelles (mitochondria and ER).

MitER can also be used to analyze the asymmetry and radial spatial distribution of organelles, which we carried out in all three cellular growth conditions. Asymmetry is expressed as the Euclidean distance between the centers of gravity of the cell and specific organelles (assuming constant densities), normalized by the average cell radius (half of the average height, length, and width of the cell), with perfect symmetry being equal to 0. We found that cells in different metabolic states show significant changes in radial asymmetry of mitochondrial distributions (Figure 5A). Asymmetry is substantially higher in fermenting cells than in respiring cells, consistent with the latter having their mitochondria more evenly distributed across the cell, preferentially at its periphery. In contrast, the ER is highly symmetric in all states, with asymmetry values below 0.2 across conditions, but it is also significantly more symmetric in respiration compared to fermentation (Figure 5B).Figure 5Organelle asymmetry and distribution in different metabolic states of S. cerevisiae(A) Mitochondrial asymmetry expressed as the Euclidean distance between the centers of gravity of the cell and mitochondria, normalized by the average cell radius.(B) ER asymmetry computed by the same metric.(C) Mitochondrial volume as a function of cell volume across conditions. Individual cell data are plotted as circles, and line plots connect the average volumes for each condition.(D) ER distribution across conditions plotted in the same manner.(E) The fraction of mitochondrial volume in the exterior 75% of the cell.(F) The mitochondrial concentration (mitochondrial volume/cell volume) in the exterior 75% of the cell.ns: p > 0.05, ∗: p ≤ 0.05, ∗∗∗: p ≤ 0.001, ∗∗∗∗: p ≤ 0.0001.Figure was created with BioRender.com.gr5.jpg344319a4565240023bb6be0648a4cb5fc35b80LOAD_COMPLETED28862222961740urn:cdn:blobs/d783/10832265/a4565240023b/gr5.jpggr5.gif75033921b835e78292b26c557572e654f7cfeNEVER_LOAD130100urn:cdn:blobs/d783/10832265/921b835e7829/gr5.gif

MitER also enables analyses of the distribution profiles of organelles by plotting their volume as a function of fractional cell volume. Based on the distribution profiles of mitochondria and ER (Figures 5C and 5D), we see the ER distributions in all metabolic states are shifted toward the outer regions of the cell relative to the mitochondrial distributions. This is evident by the fraction of organelle volume contained within the central 50% of the cell volume. Approximately 75% of the total mitochondrial volume is contained within this inner cell volume (Figure 5C), whereas less than 50% of the ER volume is contained in the same space (Figure 5D). Differences in mitochondrial distributions between metabolic states are most evident within the interior quarter (25%) of the cell, where there is a measurable decrease in the fraction of mitochondrial volume during respiration (Figure 5C), corresponding to a significant increase in fractional mitochondrial volume in the exterior 75% of the cell (closest to the plasma membrane, Figure 5E). Coupling this with the asymmetry data, we can quantify images of respiring mitochondria in yeast: predominantly located at the cell perimeter in a symmetrical mitochondrial network.

Interestingly, while the fractional mitochondrial enrichment in the outer regions of respiring cells is relatively modest (Figure 5E), when combined with the increased mitochondrial volume in this metabolic state (Figures 3B and 3C), the overall effect is a dramatic increase in mitochondrial concentration in the outermost cellular regions relative to fermenting or transitioning cells (Figure 5F). This effect is also seen when analyzing only the outer 50% region of the cell (Figure S4). With this analysis, we are able to provide quantitative descriptions of yeast mitochondrial phenotypes in different metabolic states, which helps characterize the subcellular environment more precisely.

### MitER for mammalian cells

Although MitER is optimized to analyze yeast cells, many of the measurements also prove useful for mammalian cell analysis (Figure 6). Mammalian cells are more challenging to analyze than yeast cells. Their surfaces are far more irregular than the spheroid yeast cell morphology, and as the renderings of mammalian structures can be over 1 GB, running the workflow on files this large can be prohibitively slow. Nevertheless, the workflow can be adapted to provide useful measurements for mammalian systems. Prior to cell surface estimation, the mesh can be simplified using the Decimate modifier in Blender. This modifier simplifies the vertex count while preserving overall topology. With this strategy, prior to analysis, we reduced organelle renderings to 20% of their original size by setting the vertex ratio to 0.05. These smaller files could then be opened in ParaView for cell surface estimation. The estimation of cell surface area and volume by the ER signal still holds true in mammalian cells as the ER runs parallel to the mammalian plasma membrane.14 Therefore, the Delaunay triangulation protocol can be adapted to compute these more complicated cell shapes (Figure 6A). Even for highly complicated mammalian organelle networks, MitER and Imaris produce the same volume (Figure 6B) and surface area (Figure 6C) measurements. Furthermore, overlap volumes computed by MitER are highly correlated with those reported by Imaris for both mitochondrial-ER and peroxisome-ER interactions (Figure 6D).Figure 6Using MitER to analyze mammalian systems(A) Delaunay 3D triangulation in ParaView can be used to approximate the cell surface from the (i) ER signal in mammalian systems with several modifications (outlined in STAR Methods). In brief, a filter is applied to the (ii) Delaunay surface that (iii) removes polygons with large volumes as these polygons tend to smooth the irregularities we aim to preserve in the topology of the mammalian cell surface. (iv) Another filter is applied to clean up the remaining polygons that are long and narrow, so they are missed by the initial volume filter.(B) MitER and Imaris produce the same volume measurements for mammalian organelle renderings.(C) MitER and Imaris produce the same surface area measurements for mammalian organelle renderings.(D) MitER overlap volumes are highly correlated with those reported by Imaris for both mitochondrial-ER and peroxisome-ER interactions.(E) Simplification of the mammalian surface is performed by applying a Remesh modifier prior to the computation of organelle distribution. (i) The simplified cell surface (white) lacks the protrusions common to mammalian cells (blue) allowing for (ii) neater sectioning (white) of organelles such as mitochondria (blue).(F) The volumes of each resulting section are compared to the total mammalian cell volume to determine the fraction of cell volume in each section, and the mitochondrial volumes in each resulting section are compared to the total cellular mitochondrial volume to determine the fraction of mitochondrial volume in each section.gr6.jpg382032896bcb806c4fd570ddf28bcb79b5d977LOAD_COMPLETED33533333744740urn:cdn:blobs/d783/10832265/896bcb806c4f/gr6.jpggr6.gif7694127fd74a718a0e07ea99a142749513ee1NEVER_LOAD101100urn:cdn:blobs/d783/10832265/27fd74a718a0/gr6.gif

MitER can be adapted to provide measurements regarding organelle distribution in mammalian systems. As mammalian cell morphologies are far more complex than those found in yeast cells, simply scaling down the cell topology is not appropriate for sectioning the cell. To address this issue, we can again turn to the Remesh modifier in Blender, this time specifying a voxel size of 1 (as opposed to the voxel size of 0.03 used for Remeshing cellular components to aid with Boolean operations). By specifying a larger voxel size, we take advantage of the loss of topological detail and obtain an estimate of the mammalian cell body without the large protrusions most problematic for cell sectioning (Figure 6Ei). This simplified cell body estimate can then be duplicated, scaled down, and nested to obtain concentric volumes to section the cell (Figure 6Eii). The volumes of each resulting section are then compared to the total mammalian cell volume to determine the fraction of cell volume in each section, and the mitochondrial volumes in each resulting section are compared to the total cellular mitochondrial volume to determine the fraction of mitochondrial volume in each section (Figure 6F). Therefore, while MitER could be further optimized for mammalian cells, as it stands, it is very well suited to study inter-organelle contacts in mammalian systems.

### MitER for organelle dynamics

Single-cell measurements obtained with MitER can be particularly powerful in the context of time-lapse studies of organelle dynamics. Population-level data of these dynamic phenomena, while useful, can miss the finer shifts organelles undergo as they switch between metabolic states. We employed the MitER workflow to time-lapse data of yeast undergoing the transition from fermentation to respiration. Using MitER, it is possible to track changes in volume, surface area, and inter-organelle contacts in single cells across time. In this proof-of-concept experiment, we imaged yeast cells initially grown in glucose and then switched into media containing glycerol and ethanol as the sole carbon sources 1 h prior to imaging. We imaged the cells every 45 min for 12 h (Figure 7A). We then selected 6 cells from the population, rendered them in MitoGraph, and analyzed them with the MitER script in Blender. Using these data, we can make detailed analyses of mitochondrial dynamics, including changes in volume (Figure 7B), surface area (Figure 7C), and mito-ER contact surface area changes (Figure 7C) over time. Looking at cell A and cell B (Videos S1 and S2 respectively), we observe that both subtle (Cell A) and profound (Cell B) volume and surface area changes over time are captured by MitER analysis. Furthermore, in all cells, changes in mito-ER contacts do not simply follow changes in mitochondrial surface area (Figure 7C) but rather seem to depend on other unknown subcellular phenomena, which warrants future investigation. ## Discussion

In this study, we developed an open-source image analysis pipeline for the quantification of the morphology and cellular distribution of mitochondria and mito-ER contacts. In constructing our workflow, we aimed to maximize the number of meaningful measurements we could obtain without the need for complicated sample preparation. Our pipeline allows for simple 3D segmentation and estimation of the cell surface from the ER fluorescent signal. To demonstrate the functionality and accuracy of our method, we analyzed single yeast cells in three different metabolic states.

Our pipeline produced measurements consistent with both previous studies and with peer-reviewed methods such as MitoGraph.8 We observed an increase in both mitochondrial volume and surface area in respiration relative to fermentation and an increased number of mito-ER contacts in respiration relative to both fermenting and transitioning cells. These findings indicate that mitochondria increase in surface area and volume prior to increasing contact with the ER. We also found that in all conditions, most of the mitochondrial volume exists in the periphery of the cell, but respiring cells exhibit a higher concentration of peripheral mitochondria compared to fermenting cells. Fermenting cells, on the other hand, display the most asymmetry in mitochondrial distribution. These differences in mitochondrial configurations could be crucial cellular adaptations to different metabolic states, and the mitochondrial morphological transitions observed in cells shifting from growing in glucose to growing in glycerol and ethanol are likely main contributors to the lag in growth as cells adapt to the new growth condition.

MitER can be used to screen large numbers of cells with minimal user input. Aside from cell segmentation and pre-processing, the workflow is entirely automated. Therefore, MitER is well suited to investigate disease processes that disrupt mitochondrial behavior such as dysfunctional mitophagy and altered fission and fusion processes. This workflow could also be used to characterize and design yeast mitochondria for optimal chemical production, as mitochondria are common targets of metabolic engineering for biosynthetic applications.15,16

MitER can serve as a powerful substitute for colocalization measurements to analyze the contacts between very small structures as it is only limited by the resolution of the microscope used for imaging. MitER is also well suited to analyze other inter-organelle contacts such as the peroxisome-ER interactions (Figure 6D), mitochondria-vacuole interactions, and organelle contact with the nucleus. Furthermore, the program allows for the measurement of discrete organelles when only one subcellular structure is marked in addition to the cell surface and when overlap measurements are of no interest.

In conclusion, freely available MitER has many of the commonly used capabilities found in costly commercial software that would help mitigate rising expenses in academic and industrial labs.17 This workflow addresses the growing need for open-source image analysis tools for organelle morphology and interactions and enables a better quantitative understanding of the complexity of the subcellular environment.

### Limitations of the study

As is the case with most imaging analysis techniques, the quality of the results depends on the quality of the imaging. If there is a substantial offset between fluorescent channels, both the colocalization and rendering results will be affected. Additionally, rendering-based approaches will not compensate for poor fluorophore expression. A strong fluorophore signal is a prerequisite to both reliable renderings and colocalization measurements.

In this pipeline, we use MitoGraph to produce our renderings due to its relative ease of use and it being an open-source program. MitoGraph, however, is sensitive to fluorophore signal intensity relative to the background, and poor signal can lead to an underestimation of the volume of a structure. On occasion, the software may not register any structure in the specified ROI. Some commercial programs have machine learning tools to compensate for low signal and to produce high-quality renderings, but commercial rendering software is often prohibitively expensive.

Manual 3D segmentation and application of the Delaunay 3D filter prevents this workflow from being completely automatic. The requirement that the user processes each cell individually is the bottleneck that limits the maximum number of cells that can be practically analyzed. However, this also provides the opportunity for quality control to ensure minimal background, acceptable structure rendering, and proper channel alignment. This step also allows for single cells to be precisely sectioned from renderings of cell clusters—an asset during live-cell imaging of budding yeast. Future efforts to automate the segmentation and filtering steps would enable the use of MitER in high-throughput applications, but it would be necessary to introduce quality control algorithms to maintain the same high-quality results.

### Experimental model and study participant details

#### Saccharomyces cerevisiae strain construction

The background strain used in this study is CEN.PK2-1C. To label the mitochondria, we expressed GFPmut3 fused on its N-terminus with the mitochondrial localization signal (the first 26 amino acids) of COX4. To label the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), we expressed mCherry fused on its N-terminus to an ER signal sequence (SS) and on its C-terminus to the HDEL ER retention signal.10 Constructs Cox4-GFPmut3 and pTPI1-SS-mCherry-HDEL (Addgene #133647) were linearized with pmeI and pacI, respectively, and integrated into the HIS3 and TRP1 genomic loci, respectively. Cox4-GFPmut3 is flanked by a TPI1 promoter and a CYC1 terminator (Figure S5). SS-mCherry-HDEL (Addgene #133647) is flanked by a TDH3 promoter and an ADH1 terminator. To further label Mmm1p, we integrated GFPmut3 following the endogenous Mmm1 along with HIS3 (Figure S6). Sequential strain transformations were done for each construct using the basic lithium acetate transformation protocol19 resulting in strain yTK32 (MATa; leu2-3_112; ura3-52; MAL2-8c; SUC10) marking mitochondria and ER and strain yTK55 (MATa; leu2-3_112; ura3-52; MAL2-8c; SUC10) marking Mmm1p and ER. Transformant colonies were selected on dropout media plates: synthetic complete (SC)-histidine or SC-tryptophan, as appropriate.

#### Mammalian strain construction

MRC-5 primary human lung fibroblast cells (ATCC CCL-171) were cultured at 37°C with 5% CO2 in media containing high glucose DMEM, 10% FBS, penicillin and streptomycin. To visualize organelles, fluorescent plasmids were transfected into cells. Mito-BFP (Addgene #49151) was used for visualization of mitochondria at 300 ng/mL, GFP-Sec61b (Addgene #15108) was used for visualization of the ER at 300 ng/mL. Transfections were carried out by first incubating our desired plasmids with 3 mL of X-tremeGENE HP DNA transfection reagent (Sigma-Aldrich) per 1 mg of DNA, diluted in Opti-MEM (Life Technologies). After 20 min at room temperature, the mixture was added dropwise to cells containing fresh warmed Opti-MEM. These cells were incubated at 37°C with 5% CO2 for 5.5 h prior to trypsinization and re-seeding into 35mm glass bottom microscope dishes (MatTek).

### Method details

#### Yeast culture and imaging

#### Single time point

Yeast cells were grown overnight in autoclaved and filtered synthetic complete (SC) media containing 2% glucose (Glu) and SC media containing 3% glycerol and 2% ethanol (GE). A single colony from a YPD plate containing yTK32 was inoculated into SC-Glu media and grown overnight in 24 well plates. In order to catch the cells during the mid-exponential phase, this overnight culture was inoculated into 1 mL SC-GE in 1:50, 1:100, and 1:500 dilutions. The overnight culture was inoculated into 1 mL SC-Glu in 1:500, 1:1000, 1:2000 dilutions. These cultures were set to grow overnight at 30°C in 24 well plates at 200 RPM. Once the cells reached mid-exponential phase (between OD600 = 4 and 5), cells were diluted 1:50 in 1 mL of either SC-Glu or SC-GE in a fresh 24-well plate. Cells that grew overnight in Glu medium were used to inoculate GE and Glu media whereas cells that grew overnight in GE medium were used to inoculate GE medium only. Following inoculation, cells were incubated at room temperature without shaking for 3 h and then adhered to 96-well plates pretreated with concanavalin A. To image cells, 96-well glass bottom plates (Cellvis, P96-1.5H-N) were pretreated for cell adhesion by pipetting 15 mL of 1 mg/mL concanavalin A (ConA) in 20 mM NaOAc and centrifuged for 1 min at 1,000 RPM. Plates were then incubated at room temperature for 1 h. Following incubation, wells were washed twice with 100 mL phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) and allowed to dry for 1 h at room temperature, after removing most of the last wash volume. Once the wells were dry, 50 mL of the diluted cells (see above) were added to each well and the plate was centrifuged for 2 min at 1,000 RPM.

As cell stains sometimes interact with concanavalin A, yeast for studies involving dye were adhered using poly-L-lysine (Sigma). For these trials, the 96-well plate was pretreated with 50 μL of cold poly-L-Lysine and spun down for 1 min at 1000 RPM. After 5 min of incubation, the solution was removed by aspiration and washed twice with PBS. The treated wells were then allowed to dry for 2 h before introducing cells and media.

To verify the ER-derived cell surface estimates, cell membranes were stained with MemBrite 640/660 kit (Biotium) following cell adhesion to the 96 well plates. Fresh 1X dilutions of pre-staining buffer and dye solution were prepared in PBS from the 1000X stocks provided in the kit. 50 μL of 1X pre-staining buffer was added to each well and cells were incubated for 5 min at 37°C. The liquid was vacuumed from the plate and replaced with 50 μL 1X dye solution. Again, the cells were incubated at 37°C for 5 min. The dye was vacuumed from the plate and the cells were washed twice with PBS. Cells were incubated in 100 μL PBS for imaging.

Live yeast single time point imaging was performed on a Nikon W1 SoRa at room temperature using a 63× oil objective (NA = 1.49) with 4× magnification for a pixel size of 0.027 μm. Yeast cells were imaged in 3D (40–70 z sections, 0.2 μm apart). The GFPmut3 and mCherry fluorophores were excited with 488 nm and 561 nm illumination respectively. The MemBrite cell surface stain was excited at 640 nm. Theoretical resolutions for downstream sample analysis were calculated using the following equations:

For Axial Resolution: 0.4 λ/NA

For Lateral Resolution: 1.4 λ ⋅ η/NA2 (with η = 1.515 for the refractive index of oil).

Using the equations above, theoretical lateral resolution for the wavelengths (λ) 488nm and 561nm were calculated to be 131 nm and 151 nm respectively. Theoretical axial resolution for the wavelengths 488nm and 561nm were calculated to be 347 nm and 399 nm respectively. The volume cutoff of 0.009 μm3 used for filtering contacts was computed from the product of the squared theoretical lateral limit of resolution and the axial resolution for mCherry.

Single timepoint yeast images were denoised using Nikon Elements and then processed in MitoGraph to obtain 3D renderings. For each single cell, the ROI was copied across channels in order to keep the resulting renderings aligned. The cell surface was estimated using a Delaunay 3D filter on the rendering of the ER channel or on the rendering of the cell surface channel if the cell surface was marked with MemBrite.

To validate the use of MitoGraph, these same images were rendered using Imaris’ default background subtraction to detect surfaces. Surfaces were rendered individually for each fluorescent channel and then exported for further analysis in ParaView and Blender.

#### Timelapse

A single colony from a YPD plate containing yTK32 was inoculated into SC-Glu media and grown overnight in 24 well plates. The overnight culture was inoculated into 1 mL SC-Glu in 1:500, 1:1000, 1:2000 dilutions. These cultures were set to grow overnight at 30°C in 24 well plates at 200 RPM. Once the cells reached mid-exponential phase (OD600 = 4.5), cells were diluted 1:50 in SC-Glu in a fresh 24-well plate. Cells were then adhered to 96-well plates pretreated with concanavalin A. One hour prior to imaging, adhered cells were washed three times with 150 μL GE media, leaving at least 50 μL of media in the well each time to avoid cell stress. Yeast were then imaged in 200 μL of GE media.

Live yeast timelapse images were acquired on the Nikon AX NSPARC using an Apo TIRF 60× Oil objective (NA = 1.49) with a 5× magnification for a pixel size of 0.057 μm. Yeast cells were imaged in 3D (40–70 z sections, 0.17 μm apart). The GFPmut3 and mCherry fluorophores were excited with 488 nm and 561 nm illumination respectively.

Yeast timelapse images were deconvolved using Nikon Elements and then processed in MitoGraph to obtain 3D renderings. For each single cell, the ROI was copied across channels and timepoints in order to keep the resulting renderings aligned. The cell surface was estimated using a Delaunay 3D filter on the rendering of the ER channel.

#### Mammalian culture and imaging

24-48 h post transfection, the cells were washed with PBS and fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde, 0.05% glutaraldehyde in PBS. Samples were then permeabilized with ice-cold methanol for 20 min at −20°C then blocked for 20 min in PBS containing 0.01% Triton, 5% goat serum and 5% human serum. Cells were then ready for overnight primary staining with PTPIP51 (Sigma-Aldrich, HPA009975) diluted 1:750 in block or with Pex14 (Abcam, ab183885) diluted 1:500, for mitochondria and peroxisome imaging, respectively.

Following washes, Alexa Fluor 647 was diluted 1:2,000 in block and incubated with the cells for 1 h. Images were acquired on a Nikon W1-SoRa at 60x with a 2.8× SoRa magnification. 17-point Z-stacks were taken of every image with a Z-step of 0.19μm. Nikon Elements was used for denoising and deconvolution of images.

Mammalian images were rendered using Imaris’ background subtraction (local contrast) automatic settings. Automatic threshold values were used without adjustments.

#### Running the MitER workflow

The following is a step-by-step guide on how to run the MitER workflow on .obj or .VTK files.

#### Requirements

(1)ParaView (https://www.paraview.org/)(2)Blender (version 3.6 https://download.blender.org/release/Blender3.6/)(3)RStudio (https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/)

#### Section cells and estimate cell surface in ParaView

(1)Open surface .VTK or .obj files in ParaView. Select apply and then hide all except your renderings of interest using the eye icons.(2)If your rendering has multiple cells in it, select single cells for downstream analysis.(3)Click Select cells through (shortcut -f) - > click and drag to define ROI -> copy active selection -> extract selection.

Note: Make sure to keep your ROI the same for multiple channels of the same cell.

#### Estimate cell surface by applying a Delaunay 3D filter to the cell surface signal or ER signal respectively

For yeast cells use the following procedure.1.Cell or ER signal -> Filters -> Alphabetical -> Delaunay 3D - > ApplyFor mammalian cells use the following procedure1.Cell or ER signal -> Filters -> Alphabetical -> Delaunay 3D - > Apply2.Delaunay3D1 -> Filters -> Alphabetical -> CellSize1 -> ApplyThis step calculates the volumes of the polygons making up the Delaunay triangulation mesh3.CellSize1 -> Filters -> Alphabetical -> Threshold -> ApplySet the threshold to select only volumes below 0.1 as the polygons with larger volumes bridge the irregularities native to the mammalian cell periphery4.Threshold1 -> Filters -> Alphabetical -> Mesh Quality -> ApplyThis step allows for the calculation of user-defined metrics. Set the Triangle, Quad, and Tet Quality measures to Radius Ratio using the dropdown menus.5.MeshQuality1 -> Filters -> Alphabetical -> Threshold -> ApplySet the threshold category to quality and select only polygons with a Radius Ratio below 40. This will remove the long and narrow polygons not caught by the original volume filter.

Note: You can add these filters to your favorites for easy access during analysis of many cells

Ensuring only the channels you wish to analyze are visible within the frame

File -> Export Scene -> Save as.x3d File.

#### Obtaining raw data from blender

Important: For the script to run, 3D toolbox needs to be enabled

#### Initial setup

(1)Create a folder on your desktop called MitER and put the MitER scripts here.(2)Open Blender and select the following:Edit -> Preferences -> Add-ons-> Search and select Mesh: 3D-Print Toolbox

#### Running the blender script

(1)In Blender, select Scripting from the main toolbar.(2)In the scripting window select the following:⋅Text -> Open -> Navigate to MitEREngine.py in the folder on your desktop and select it.(3)Once the script is open, click run and select directory (folder) containing the .x3d files you want to analyze.(4)Your output will auto-populate .csv files within a data folder in the MitER directory on your desktop.

#### Analyzing raw data in R

(1)Open the MitER Tools R script from your MitER desktop directory and set the path your data folder.(2)Run the script and the resulting collated .csv files will output into your data folder.(3)From here you can plot the data as you see fit.

### Quantification and statistical analysis

Real-time fluorescent measurements were collected using a Nikon W1 SoRa and a Nikon AX NSPARC, rendered using MitoGraph, and analyzed using a custom-made Python pipeline developed for Blender (https://github.com/tkichuk/MitER). The data was processed further using custom R scripts as described in the main text and also provided on GitHub. Statistical analysis was performed using the t-test function in the R package “ggpubr” using the following cutoffs for significance: ns: p > 0.05, ∗: p ≤ 0.05, ∗∗: p ≤ 0.01, ∗∗∗: p ≤ 0.001, ∗∗∗∗: p ≤ 0.0001. Schematics were designed using BioRender, example images were taken from ParaView and violin plots, scatterplots, and boxplots were generated in R.
